new_camps.name: Star Lake
new_camps.why: The usual base for Star Peak: water at the door, the ridge within reach for a full day, and a downhill carry out on day three.
new_camps.water: The lake and its outlet stream.
new_camps.capacity: Room for a few tents on the benches around the shore.
new_camps.permit: No limited-entry permit; keep tents 200 ft from the water.
new_camps.notes: About 7.5 miles and 3,500 ft from the West Fork Buttermilk trailhead; the upper trail is brushy, so the carry is slower than the mileage suggests. Camping just below Fish Creek Pass is the only other option parties mention.

camps.name: Star Lake
camps.why: The standard basecamp: the scree bowl to the summit starts right above it, and it has water, so the summit day is a light-pack outing.

camps.name: Cooney Lake
camps.why: The one-night camp for this route: lots of sites around the north shore, water, and the pass to the southeast ridge about a mile above. Bugs are bad in July.

camps.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
camps.why: Reached from the Gold Creek side, not this trailhead. Used by parties linking other crest peaks; not slept at on the Foggy Dew plan.

new_camps.name: Company Creek Trail camp near the leave-trail point
new_camps.why: Day one is short after the boat, so parties stop near where the route leaves the trail and start the steep brush and slabs fresh the next morning.
new_camps.capacity: Informal; room for a small party.
new_camps.permit: Stehekin backcountry permit from the NPS.
new_camps.notes: Many parties instead cross to the Devore Creek trail and sleep at Bird Creek Camp, which cuts the next day's off-trail work; this plan's route goes over the Bird Lakes pass instead. Night one is the least documented of the trip.

new_camps.name: High bivy in the Bird Lakes basin
new_camps.why: Sleeping in the basin below the east face puts the climb a short walk away and keeps the summit day light; the last water is a trickle near the top larches.
new_camps.water: A small seep near the highest larches; carry water from the lakes.
new_camps.capacity: A few flat spots near the highest larch trees, about 200 ft above the creek.
new_camps.permit: Stehekin backcountry permit; bivy only, no fires.
new_camps.notes: Elevation is approximate. Reached after crossing the roughly 7,200 ft pass above Bird Lakes. Parties sleep here the night before and the night after the climb.

plan_conflict: Plan sends parties over the Bird Lakes pass, but most reports reach Tupshin from Bird Creek Camp on the Devore Creek trail; night 1 is not confirmed.

new_camps.name: Swamp Creek area camp on the PCT
new_camps.why: The end of an easy 8.5 miles on the PCT and the last good water and flat ground before the steep off-trail climb the next morning.
new_camps.capacity: Several sites near the creek crossing.
new_camps.notes: Also the usual first camp for Needle Peak and Lyall. Logs across Agnes and Spruce Creeks start day two.

new_camps.name: Upper Blue Basin camp
new_camps.why: The first flat ground after a brutal brush, talus and slab climb; stopping here splits the carry before the final move to the pass.
new_camps.water: Snowmelt and small streams in the basin.
new_camps.notes: Off-trail, no maintained path; expect a slow day two. Reports of this basin are thin.

new_camps.name: High camp near Icy-Spruce Pass
new_camps.why: The high camp for the south ridge: it makes the 8-9 hour summit push possible from camp and is the base you return to before hiking out.
new_camps.water: Snow patches or a nearby tarn; check in late season.
new_camps.notes: Reached after about 1,760 ft of steep ground above Upper Blue Basin. Parties camp on the divide or on the col below the peak.

camps.name: Bird Creek Camp
camps.why: The only designated camp on the upper Devore Creek trail, and the base parties climb Flora from; sleeping here again saves carrying the pack up the peak.

camps.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
camps.why: Valley camps by the landing and shuttle; not used on this plan, but the fallback if the boat or shuttle gets you in too late to start up the trail.

camps.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
camps.why: The working camp for Needle: the unmaintained trail to the north ridge leaves from here, so the long summit day starts at the door and ends back at the tent.

camps.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
camps.why: Landing-area camps near Stehekin, only for a missed shuttle or late boat; this plan goes straight to High Bridge and up the valley.

camps.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
camps.why: Where the shuttle drops you; fine for a late arrival but it adds nine miles to the next morning, so most parties push on to Swamp Creek the same day.

camps.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
camps.why: Four miles short of Swamp Creek; use it if you arrive late or tire, and accept a longer approach to the north ridge the next morning.

camps.name: Ridgeline camp above 5,400 ft
camps.why: A higher camp on the ridge shortens the summit day but costs a steep brushy carry from Swamp Creek; few parties use it.

camps.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
camps.why: After the Fourth Creek Pass descent and ford, sites near the creek give water and the shortest bushwhack to the ridge; the long day out starts from here.

camps.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
camps.why: Sleep beside the road the night before to start at the Beverly Turnpike trailhead early, rather than driving in the dark from town.

plan_conflict: Plan calls it a basin bivy on the slope below the ridge, but parties on this approach sleep in the Ingalls Creek valley near the Fourth Creek junction.

camps.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
camps.why: Flat ground in the basin puts the approach couloir within an hour of camp and cuts the summit day; boulders give some shelter.

camps.name: Lower basin below Argonaut's north face
camps.why: The lower part of the same basin: easier to reach after the Mountaineer Creek bushwhack and nearer water, but a longer morning to the couloir.

camps.name: Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence camp
camps.why: Where Fourth Creek meets the Ingalls trail, just before the bushwhack up to the face; the standard camp for the south side and a good spot to store gear.

camps.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
camps.why: Other flat sites along Ingalls Creek; farther up or down the trail, so a longer approach or a longer hike out than the confluence.

camps.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
camps.why: Road camps on the drive in; sleep here to start the Beverly trailhead hike at first light rather than driving in the dark.

plan_conflict: Two camps on file are both marked main for this plan; only the confluence camp is kept as main.

camps.name: Snow Lakes
camps.why: A permit-friendlier base than the core: about 6.5 miles in, shorter than the full core carry, with the summit day continuing above Lake Viviane.

camps.name: Nada Lake
camps.why: A lower camp, about 1,700 ft up; for a late start or a short first day, but it makes the next day to the summit much longer.

plan_conflict: Plan sends parties to the core near Perfection or Inspiration Lake (a Core permit); route guides and trip reports use Snow Lakes as the base.

camps.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
camps.why: Established sites by the water, about two hours below the summit ridge; camp here rather than carry cross-country to higher ground.

plan_conflict: Plan puts camp at a cross-country 7,100 ft site; parties report sleeping at the Caroline lakes (about 6,200 ft).

new_camps.name: Colchuck Lake campsites
new_camps.why: The base for the wall: 4.3 miles in, with the basin below it about an hour beyond the north end of the lake, so a slow aid day starts early.
new_camps.capacity: Established sites along the shore, most on the trail side.
new_camps.permit: Colchuck Zone overnight permit by lottery (May 15 to Oct 31); Northwest Forest Pass.
new_camps.notes: Permits are hard to get; without one the climb is a long car-to-car day, which is rarely done on aid.

camps.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
camps.why: The basecamp for the couloir: 4 miles in, and it saves the pre-dawn walk-in; an overnight permit is needed and hard to draw.

camps.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
camps.why: If no lake permit, sleep on the road the night before and start the long summit day from the trailhead in the small hours.

camps.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
camps.why: Used for the Dragontail routes, not this one; a colder, windier night above the lake that is no closer to the couloir.

camps.name: Colchuck Lake
camps.why: The south end of the lake is closer to the glacier and the couloir but has fewer flat sites than the trail side.

plan_conflict: Two camps on file are both marked main; only the lake campsites are kept as main, and the roadside campgrounds are the night before.

camps.name: Crystal Creek basin below the Southwest Rib
camps.why: Informal camping near the toe of the rib: running water to about 5,800 ft, no permit, and the 19-pitch climb starts from the tent.
